1.pericope_label: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth. O Lord, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O Lord, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy.

schools.summary: Take the heading for metre or musical setting, prefer thy report to thy speech, and make the tidings those of the judgment just announced.
Read the chapter as a prayer for the removal of what obstructs Christ's kingdom, and take the word heard for the voice of God rather than a report.
Set out the prophet's mingled terror and hope, and refer the hearing to the answer given in the first chapter.
Argues from the office that prophets were praying men who could lay up a stock of prayers against troublous times.

debates.question: What is the speech the prophet says he heard?

positions.position: Thy report, in the tone of the fathers telling what God did of old, which he now asks to see manifested again.
The tidings just delivered, of judgment on Judah through the Chaldeans and afterwards on the Chaldeans.
The answer given to the inquiry of the first chapter.
Not a report but the voice of God, since the sentiment that the faithful feared a report would be frigid.
Not the evangelical report of Christ's coming and sufferings, which would have been matter of joy rather than fear.

outliers.claim: Holds that the term in the heading points to metrical structure or musical setting rather than contents, and that the piece is called a prayer and not a psalm because it is throughout an account of deliverance anticipated by faith.

Argues that those acquainted with God's mind concerning things to come knew best what to pray for, and could lay up a stock of prayers in the foresight of troublous times, so serving the church by prayer when their prophesying was over.

themes: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth.
O Lord, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O Lord, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy.

3.pericope_label: God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power.

schools.summary: Render the theophany in the future and place Teman and Paran as the Edomite and southern regions, noting the ode's roots in the song of Moses.
Weigh whether the words are petition, comparison or record, and take the brightness for sunlight capable of filling the world.
Keep the past tense and bring both mountains near Sinai, calling the opening a sudden burst of poetry in the spirit of the ode.
Explains the backward look as the practice of God's people in distress, recollecting experiences and pleading them with God.

debates.question: Is the coming past or future?

positions.position: Future: God shall come from Teman, his glory covers the heavens.
Past: the God of the fathers discovered himself from Teman.
Undecided among three: a petition that God may come, a comparison with his coming of old, or a record of the giving of the law.
In Edom: Teman a city five miles from Petra where Mount Seir stood, Paran the region to the south-west.
Near Sinai: Teman a mountain not far from where the law was given, and Paran beside it.

outliers.claim: Reports a whole series of identifications for the brightness - the fire on the mount, the pillar of fire, the primogenital light of the first day, the light of the seven days - before preferring the sun in full strength because Christ is the light of the world.
Observes that the description of the theophany rests throughout on earlier lyrical accounts and that its introduction has its roots in the song of Moses.

themes: God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise.
And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power.

5.pericope_label: Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet. He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting. I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble.

schools.summary: Render the plague forward, abandon the word measure for setting the earth reeling, and take the peoples named as borderers of the Red Sea.
Reject the ark reading as strained, extend the measuring to the whole world, and identify the later deliverance as Gideon's.
Make the pestilence prepare room for Israel or else fall on Israel itself, and take Cush for tent-dwelling Arabia.

debates.question: What does the standing and measuring mean?

positions.position: The ark abiding at Gilgal while Canaan was subdued, after which the land was measured and divided by lot.
The division of the promised land among the tribes, as a conqueror divides a subdued country among his soldiers.
God's presence with Joshua, standing by while the work was done.
Neither: the ark reading is strained and frigid; God stood as one drawn erect to be seen far off, and the measuring extends to the whole world as belongs to a sovereign king.
Not measuring at all: he stands and sets the earth reeling.

debates.question: Whom does the pestilence go against?

positions.position: The nations, sent before God and his people to make way for them.
The disobedient Israelites themselves, on whom it was several times inflicted in the wilderness.
Rendered forward: the plague shall go before him and burning pestilence go forth where he sets his feet.

outliers.claim: Identifies Cushan with Ethiopia and holds the Ethiopians and Midianites to be one people, on the ground that the Midianite wife of Moses is elsewhere called an Ethiopian woman.

Adopts the reading that refers the verse to a later deliverance, naming the work by which the Jews were freed from Midian by the hand of Gideon, and explains that the prophet gathers such histories to comfort men who thought themselves rejected.

themes: Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet.
He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting.
I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble.

8.pericope_label: Was the Lord displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation? Thy bow was made quite naked, according to the oaths of the tribes, even thy word. Selah. Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers.

schools.summary: Take both crossings as in view, distinguish the baring of the bow from the shooting of arrows, and render the oaths clause as chastisements sworn by God's word.
Explain the questions as awakening the faithful to God's real design, and take the bow for every weapon of a God armed and marching to battle.
Refer the passage to the Red Sea, picture the Lord as a general at the head of his army, and keep the oath made to the fathers.

debates.question: How should the clause about the oaths be rendered?

positions.position: According to the oaths of the tribes, the performance of a promise made to the fathers.
The chastisements sworn by thy word: the noun means a rod as well as a tribe, so what is bared is a rod for the nations.

outliers.claim: Supports the reading that the bow is taken from its case rather than the arrow drawn, from a fine oriental bow with its case, quiver and arrows that he has before him.
Argues that God could not be angry with lifeless elements, so the questions are asked to awaken the faithful to consider what design God had when he dried the sea and stopped the Jordan.

themes: Was the Lord displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation?
Thy bow was made quite naked, according to the oaths of the tribes, even thy word. Selah. Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers.

10.pericope_label: The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high. The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear.

schools.summary: Read the imagery as usual in poetical accounts of divine interposition, and take the two lights as entering their dwelling so that the verse describes a darkening.
Reject the allegory of kings for the plain obedience of the mountains, and hold that the sun could not have stood unless the moon were stayed with it.
Take the inundation and the heaped waters literally, and refer the standing still to the prayer of Joshua.

debates.question: Does the standing still of sun and moon refer to Joshua's long day?

positions.position: Yes, at the prayer of Joshua when he fought the Amorites.
Yes, with the addition that the moon must have been stayed with the sun, since the same action befell both luminaries.
Yes, but the conception is of heavenly bodies shamed into ceasing their journey by the brightness of the theophany.
No: a different word is used there, the habitation is not mentioned, the history will not admit it, and the words describe not shining but its reverse.
No: the two have entered their dwelling, so the verse describes a darkening rather than a prolonged day.

debates.question: What do the trembling mountains stand for?

positions.position: Mighty peoples and nations, kings and great men struck with terror.
The mountains themselves, obeying God so as to open a way; the allegory of kings is too strained.
Poetical figures for the ease with which God accomplished arduous tasks.

outliers.claim: Reads the passage as heightening a chaotic condition into which the earth has been brought, the heaven clothing itself in darkness while the mountains writhe.
Reports with approval Calvin's remark that the arrows and spears of the Israelites are called God's own, since the people fought under his auspices.

themes: The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high.
The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear.

12.pericope_label: Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger. Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah.

schools.summary: Note the verbs are futures, take the anointed for the chosen people rather than an individual, and observe that two figures, a house and a body, are blended in the second half.
Ground the conquest in God's strength rather than Israel's courage, or else refer the march past Canaan to a judgment still to come.
Identify the anointed with Joshua, type of the Messiah, and keep the threshing figure concrete.

positions.position: Joshua, appointed to fill the place of Moses and made the instrument of the conquest.
The Messiah, as the rabbinic interpreters read it.
The chosen people themselves; few impartial Hebraists will deny this rendering is preferable.

outliers.claim: Denies the march is through Canaan at all and applies it to the antichristian jurisdiction through which the Lord will pass when he pours out the vials, adding that the clause may be read as a petition.

Asks how Israelites lately come from so miserable a bondage, and trembling through forty years in the desert, could have dared to attack so many nations, unless God had put forth the strength of his hand.

themes: Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.
Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah.

14.pericope_label: Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages: they came out as a whirlwind to scatter me: their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly. Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, through the heap of great waters.

schools.summary: Sets out why the first clause is obscure, since the nouns may mean spear or tribe and princes or villages, and marks where the poem ends.
Refuse the strained renderings of the walking through the sea, since the verb simply means to march, and read the sea as the world.
Refer the piercing to Pharaoh and his generals, or to pursuers who struck each other down in confusion.

debates.question: Who is struck through, and with whose weapons?

positions.position: Pharaoh and his host, destroyed by the very steps they took in going into the sea, or else the Canaanite princes destroying one another.
Pharaoh and his generals, or on the common reading pursuers who fell foul of one another in confusion and struck each other down.
The enemy's princes, pierced with the anointed people's own spears.

outliers.claim: Rejects the rendering that has God treading his horses in the sea as a plain solecism and the alternative as strained, since the verb simply means to go or march.
Marks a structural correction, that the prophetic poem terminates suddenly here and the new paragraph begins at the next verse rather than one verse later as the Authorised Version indicates.

themes: Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages: they came out as a whirlwind to scatter me: their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly.
Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, through the heap of great waters.

16.pericope_label: When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops. Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:

schools.summary: Renders the clause about resting quiet in the day of trouble, and changes the concessive conjunction to a causal one connecting the failures with what precedes.
Correct the construction that would derive the dread from the evidences of God's power, and defend the received verb for the fig tree while granting the botanical point.
Explain the turn from the ancient wonders back to the present desolation, and correct the natural history of the fig tree from observation.
Sets the passage between the two poles of trembling and triumphing, and describes the physical effect of the fear in detail.

debates.question: Does the verse about the failing harvests concede or explain?

positions.position: It concedes: these are the afflictions in spite of which the prophet will rejoice.
It explains: render for rather than although, since the verse connects with what precedes and sets out the affliction more fully.

debates.question: Should the fig tree be said to blossom?

positions.position: No: the tree bears no blossoms but puts forth green figs at once, so render that it shall not bring forth fruit.
No: the young figs appear as soon as the old are ripe, as he has often observed, so render that it shall not flourish.
The received word may stand, since the verb strictly means to bud and covers germinating and shooting as well as blossoming.

outliers.claim: Refers the trembling not to the judgments coming on the church's enemies, awful as those are, but to the troubles that would fall on the churches themselves beforehand.

Corrects those who connect the hearing with the preceding verse, since there was no occasion to fear at the sight of God armed for his people's salvation, and refers it back to the earlier threatenings.

themes: When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops.

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:

18.pericope_label: Yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The Lord God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds’ feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.

schools.summary: State the relation between the trembling and the exultation, and record the closing superscription as part of the text.
Set God as strength against every other support men lean on, and enumerate what that strength is given for.
Treats the last verse as a quotation from a psalm spoken in the person of the people, and the final line as a superscription.

debates.question: What is the closing line to the chief singer?

positions.position: A superscription rather than part of the ode, suggesting the prophet folded up his finished piece with that direction on it.
Part of the text, recorded without comment.

outliers.claim: Follows the Targum in reading the rejoicing as rejoicing in the Word of the Lord, and expounds that of Christ in his person, offices, relations, fulness and personal appearing.

Points out the implied contrast in calling God one's strength, since anyone is courageous while things smile on him, so that the title sets God against every other prop and is meant to hold the faithful up when they are ready to fall at every moment.

themes: Yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
The Lord God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds’ feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.
